TWO YEARS OLD CRIME.
“CAT.”
This Morning's
Criminal

Mr. Wood's first case was that of Mak Sum, charged with robbery on April 15, 1923, at Wong Nei Cheong Village. In the course of her evidence the wife of the robbed man accused the prisoner of having forced into her husband's mouth some poison which had caused his death about twelve days later, but the Crown Solicitor, Mr. Whyte Smith, said that there was some sort of suggestion that the remedies which the man had used had aggravated the injuries.
The most striking feature of to-day's Criminal Sessions was the heavy penalty imposed by Mr. J. R. Wood, the new Puisine Judge, on a man convicted of participation in a two years old robbery.

Although two years had elapsed between the time of the robbery and the arrest of the prisoner, the woman had had no difficulty in picking the man out from thirteen others at the police station. Questioned by Mr. Justice Wood she said that she would only be able to recognise the other men who took part in the robbery "partly per cent," this man she recognised "fully per cent," because he was the one who had tied her husband up. The others had not shown their forms.

The defendant pleaded not guilty this morning but in previous statements he had confessed to participation in the robbery. At the Magistracy he had stated that he had been arrested by a police-man who had told him that he was going to get him employment on a Government launch. This policeman had told him that unless he confessed he would be beaten to death.

Child stealing formed the subject of the next charge, defendant being Tam Wing Mr. Whyte Smith said that a boy had been confided to the care of a relative in Hongkong who was a tailor and to whom he was apprenticed. He disappeared on February 27 and suspicion fell on the defendant who was the adopted son of the tailor and had taken the boy out to tea on several occasions. On being questioned by the mother of the boy the defendant said "you need not be afraid, I can recover him." At the police station he had stated that he and another man had taken the boy to Macao where they had received $25 each from a "dealer in children." The boy had not been seen by his relatives since.
The jury found defendant guilty and Mr. Justiçe Wood sentenced him to ten years' hard labour and twelve strokes of the "cat."
BANISHED MEN RETURN.
DESERTS.
Three possession of arms cases and two of breaches of deportation orders were heard in the Supreme Court before His Lordship, Sir Henry Cowper Gollan, Chief Justice.
STOLEN CHILD.

The well worn excuse of a mother's funeral to which he was returning through Hongkong availed one of the deportees little. He had been deported as an "undesirable" for life and was arrested here in connection with a theft.
He was'sentenced to three years' hard labour.
The other deporbee had been arrested in connection with a robbery and was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment with hard labour.

A man who ran away from a police picket between Mongkok and Shamsuipo was found to have been in possession of a revolver and three rounds of ammunition which were picked up by the roadside. He denied the charge and said that they were the property of someone else, there having been others who ran away from the picket. The defendant was fired at five times by the police before he was brought down. Evidence was given to the effect that the defendant had thrown the weapon away as he ran.

MRS. BOWES-SMITH'S LOSSES.
FOUR MONTHS' JAIL FOR

The mystery attending the disappearance of a number of articles belonging to Mr. A. M. Bowes Smith, of "Ediville," Repulse Bay, on various dates last month was solved when the police searched, on suspicion, the abode of a young Chinese who had worked as a house coolie at the time of the thefts.
Amongst some of the stolen property received was a leather cash box coral necklace, locker and a magnifying glass.

BRITAIN STIRRED BY GRAVE SCANDAL.

Mr. H. E. Hollands informed the China Mail this morning, in response to inquiries, that the Committee has been working to get a side together for about a month. Many of the members of the team had been granted leave and, full particulars would be available, he hoped, in the course of the next few days.

Others of the last Hongkong team who have been asked if they can go include A. C. I. Bowker, Pay, Lieut. Com. Hargreaves, R.N. C.Q.M.S. Stripp, East Surrey Regt., and A. W. Ramsay of the Kowloon Cricket Club.
Shanghai may have a chance of retrieving the “Ashes” as there is a possibility of Hongkong sending up an interport cricket team, leaving on May 8 or 9.

The Rev. E. K. Quick, with his ripe experience, has been asked to be captain. He justified his being sent in to put first in the last series played here and his right-handed slow bowling brought about a separation whenever the first line of attack looked like being beaten.

Owing to the all-important question of leave it is hardly to be expected that the strongest team will be available. Still, according to the latest information, several of the team which defeated Singapore and Shanghai, in Hongkong, at the beginning of this season, are being discussed. What with the usual glorious uncertainty and the memory of Hongkong's victory in Shanghai the year before last, it would be decidedly rash to make any predictions.

Reference has already been made in the “China Mail” to the reported failure of a piecegoods dealer of fifty-eight years' standing. Other native dealers are feeling the pinch of decreased values and high rates of interest on loans with which to carry stocks.
Fears that a crisis in local commerce may follow the piecegoods slump are causing much anxiety to the mercantile community.

Before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry, at the Central Magistracy this morning, a Chinese youth was charged with evading payment of tramway fare.

SHOT IN BACK.
KOWLOON CITY ROBBERY ARRESTS.

The armed robbery in which six men secured a haul of properly valued at $525 from a hut at To Koo Ling village in the Kowloon City district provided a further development when another two arrests were made during the week-end.
TWO MORE MEN IN CUSTODY:

On the gang entering the hut at 9 p.m. last Monday, a little boy slipped away unobserved and gave timely information at the Police Station. The police quickly turned out at the hut, but found that the robbers had got away with the haul. Later, they came upon two men hiding under an embankment and they were both arrested after a chase, one of them having to be shot in the back before he surrendered.

The wounded man is still in hospital, but his confederate, who had a dagger in his possession, was formally charged before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, when he was remanded until Friday.
The two men arrested subsequently will be charged before the Magistrate in due course.
$1,300 ROBBERY.

Six men armed with knives and revolvers, secured a good haul at 6.30 yesterday morning when they visited the two upper floors of 262, Des Voeux Road, occupied by cattle and poultry dealers.
The inmates were bound and gagged and the robbers escaped with money and jewellery estimation.
The hindrances to free transport on the waterways. Stocks hitherto ordered through Hongkong import firms were piling up here. Another disadvantage is the increasing discount on Canton subsidiary silver coins, in which piecegoods are sold in the interior. This factor is tantamount to adverse exchange.
It was decided to approach the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce for assistance. A letter was to be addressed to the Chamber to-day asking for (1) the extension of the delivery period of four months by an additional six months (2) and the waiving (by the importing hongs) of the interest which would, according to contract, accrue through non-clearance within the stipulated period.

In an interview by the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," a leading merchant explained that there were over one hundred and forty firms which imported piecegoods, or incident, for account of native dealers. Old established firms might be able to help by extending the period for effecting delivery but some of the juniors might not be able to do so.

A number of gentlemen were taking steps to avert a crisis, these steps being similar to those adopted when danger threatened the yarn trade some years ago. A European expert with over twenty years' experience in the local piecegoods trade had approached the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak (chairman of the Chamber of Commerce), says the article, and Mr. Holyoak was very sympathetic.
It is hoped that a certain amount of give and take will help materially to tide matters over and with the collaboration of the banks, hopes are entertained that a solution will be forthcoming.
That the matter is one of extreme urgency is revealed in the attitude of the native bankers some of whom are stated to be pressing dealers for the payment of advances.
PIRATE ATTACK.

"PARROTS BEAK" GANG
FOILED.
LOCAL VESSELS' ESCAPE.

“Parrot's Beak,” already notorious in the annals of Canton River piracy, has been the scene of another attempt to molest two Hongkong vessels. Fortunately, the attack was frustrated, and two pirates are believed to have met their doom, after being shot and falling into the river.
Five days ago a steam launched an empty lighter out of Hongkong, bound for Wuchow, where it was to pick up a cargo of firewood.

Near “Parrot’s Beak” in the Heungshan district three particularly long rowing boats, capable of very fast speed, approached the two vessels. In each of the boats were between ten and twenty pirates most of whom were brandishing firearms of all kinds.

Going alongside the lighter, the pirates attempted to clamber on deck but were frustrated through the lighter being empty and, therefore, standing high out of the water. The gang made several efforts to board the lighter. Meanwhile the coxswain of the launch had ordered his crew to open fire. Returning the fire, the pirates made off as fast as they could with the launch steaming away in the other direction.
The coxswain reports that he noticed two pirates fall into the water as though they had been shot.
